newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Cavallo hits back on postal indictment.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Cavallo hits back on postal indictment.

text.p: Former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, stung by an indictment for abuse of power, arrived home Wednesday firing back accusations at judges and at the government of President Carlos Menem.

Even angrier after being turned away from the VIP lounge at Buenos Aires' Ezeiza airport on his return from the United States, the former minister told waiting reporters: "It's enough for a public official to fight corruption or tax evasion or smuggling for him to be put on trial."

Cavallo, the widely-praised reformist minister sacked by Menem last July and now campaigning for a seat in Congress, was indicted for intervening in a tender for postal services for state mortgage lender Banco Hipotecario in 1993.

He annulled it and gave the contract to state post office Encotesa at 40 cents a letter, rather than renew a contract held by private postal firm OCASA at $1.80 per letter, saving Banco Hipotecario hundreds of thousands of dollars a month.
OCASA is owned by postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran, Cavallo's archenemy whom he has accused in Congress and in the media of being the head of organized crime in Argentina.

A federal judge accused Cavallo of "interests incompatible with public office" and said he did not rule out that Cavallo had made some personal profit. The court also pointed out that Encotesa was then run by a close friend of Cavallo.
The case was brought by OCASA. Yabran is also suing Cavallo for libel, as are Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan whom he accuses of protecting Yabran.

Cavallo, who has about 20 court cases pending, many of them for slander, has also turned on President Menem, accusing him Wednesday of being "afraid" of Yabran and of "lying" about Yabran's business interests. Menem denies reports that he is a friend of Yabran -- but has been contradicted by his ex-wife.

Cavallo's attack on Menem earned him a sharp reprimand from Corach, who accused his one-time cabinet colleague of "disloyalty to the man who has transformed this country and whom he served for seven years as a minister."
